sources.news_title: We haven’t seen the last of the major tech outages
sources.text:
Over the last week or so, we have seen a nationwide FAA ground stop, a multi-day Outlook outage that brought entire companies to a standstill, and a banking outage at JPMorgan Chase. But the consensus is that there are more to come. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN:
We haven’t seen the last of the major tech outages
Microsoft and the US government agree there are more outages to come.
“The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.”
Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning about further outages on CBS News’ Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan, but sounded a much more ominous tone.
“I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn’t the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks … The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now.”
While the outages over the last week were believed to be caused by cyberattacks, Smith said that AI has made it easier to find flaws, “and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems,” he said.
The last few months have also seen an increase in attacks on government and commercial systems, including those at the USDA, JP Morgan, and supermarkets.
Whether outages are brought on by AI-assisted hackers or human error during the rush to patch an aging system, one thing seems certain: there will be more in the coming months.
Update November 22nd: Added clarification that Smith was speaking on Face the Nation, not to CBS generally.

sources.news_title: DNI Jay Clayton Warns Americans to Prepare for More Technology Outages — Says There Will Be “Bumps in the Road” as Government and Corporations “Upgrade Their Systems” * The Gateway Pundit * by Jim Hᴏft
sources.text:
America’s top intelligence official is warning the American people that the recent wave of technological disruptions may not be over.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton appeared on CNN’s State of the Union Sunday, warning that Americans should anticipate additional service interruptions as government agencies and private corporations overhaul their aging technology infrastructure amid the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence.
The warning comes just days before Thanksgiving, following widespread outages that disrupted the nation’s banking system, grounded thousands of flights, crippled Microsoft services, and even affected the National Security Agency’s internal communications network.
Clayton told CNN host Dana Bash that Americans should expect “bumps in the road” as institutions invest in modernizing their systems and strengthening cybersecurity.
Clayton compared the process to renovating a house, there will be unexpected problems, and stressed that the upgrades are necessary for both performance and cybersecurity. He rejected the idea that recent incidents were a coordinated or state-sponsored cyberattack, a position he and other officials have repeated for days.
Jay Clayton: “The American people should understand that a great deal of our digital infrastructure is dated. It is—it is old. It has been built out over three decades or more. We are in a period of technological step change, both in terms of what people refer to as models, applications, and the like, and in computing power. And in that technological step change, our systems are going to need to be upgraded.
They’re going to need to be upgraded for performance and for cybersecurity. And as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, and interruptions in service. That is going to happen.
The American people should also understand that cyber threats are real. If you go back to 2020, there were almost 800,000 cyber incidents reported to the FBI.
That is—that is up to 1 million in the most recent data. And this is going to continue.
The good news, the very good news, is we lead the world in both the technology—the compute, the models, the application—and in cybersecurity. And we’re going to need to continue to do that.”

sources.news_title: US intelligence chief warns of more technology outages amid AI-driven upgrades
sources.text:
US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has warned that further technology outages may strike the country as private corporations and government agencies modernise infrastructure and fortify cybersecurity defences.
Speaking on CNN's "State of the Union", Clayton cautioned that the public should prepare for temporary service interruptions whilst institutions invest heavily in upgrading digital systems to adapt to advancements in artificial intelligence (AI).
"The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road," Clayton said.
He noted that organisations are actively addressing the transitions to limit long-term fallout.
Cyberattack assessments
The caution follows a series of high-profile technical failures that disrupted commercial flights, digital enterprise services, and retail banking transactions across the country, involving the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Microsoft Outlook, and JPMorgan Chase.
Federal officials have largely dismissed speculation linking the incidents to a coordinated foreign cyberattack or AI-driven sabotage, stating that independent assessments point to distinct, isolated technical faults.
The warning coincided with fresh travel chaos on Sunday as Delta Air Lines encountered nationwide flight delays stemming from an operational breakdown at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, its primary hub.
The FAA initially issued a ground stop for Atlanta-bound flights before instituting a ground delay programme, which caused departure delays averaging nearly an hour throughout the morning.
Delta attributed the operational disruption to a software malfunction in its automated system used to calculate aircraft weight and balance before take-off.
"Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation," the carrier confirmed in an official statement.

sources.news_title: Clayton says public should expect tech disruptions amid upgrades but remain ‘resilient’
sources.text:
U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the public should continue to expect “glitches, gaps, and interruptions in service” as technology systems upgrade in the era of artificial intelligence.
Clayton appeared on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday to address the series of outages and technological disruptions that have hit the United States throughout the past two weeks. In the wake of disruptions affecting systems such as Outlook, U.S. air traffic control, and banking giants, Clayton told the outlet these gaps are going to continue to occur because of AI model and computing updates.
Recommended Stories
“We are in a period of technological step change – both in terms of what people refer to as models, applications, and the like, and in computing power. And in that technological step change, our systems are going to need to be upgraded. They’re going to need to be upgraded for performance and for cybersecurity. And as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service. That is going to happen,” Clayton said.
The national intelligence director also told the outlet cybersecurity threats “are real” and are “going to continue.”
“The good news, the very good news, is we lead the world in both the technology, the compute, the models, the application, and in cybersecurity. And we’re going to need to continue to do that,” Clayton said.
Throughout the snowballing technological issues that have gripped the nation in the past two weeks, concerns among the public have flurried on social media, with some members of the public stockpiling water and canned food in preparation for a worst-case scenario.
However, President Donald Trump has called on the public to “relax,” telling stockpilers that “everything’s good” during his trip to China.
When asked if Americans should be stockpiling food, Clayton called the American people “resilient,” adding, “as we have this technological step change, we will handle it as a country.”
TRUMP TELLS STOCKPILERS ‘RELAX, EVERYTHING’S GOOD,’ CALLS OUTAGES ‘INDIVIDUAL EVENTS’
“America is the most amazing and resilient place, and we have been living with interruptions. Let’s give ourselves some credit. Let’s go back to COVID, other things; Americans fought their way through these terrible things in an incredibly resilient way,” Clayton said.
He clarified that the current situation is “not at all” like the level of the COVID-19 lockdowns.

sources.news_title: DNI Clayton Says Recent Tech Outages Were ‘Not Coordinated’ Or ‘State-Sponsored’
sources.text:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told “This Week” host Jonathan Karl during a Sunday interview that a recent string of major technology outages was neither coordinated nor state-sponsored, but declined to identify who was behind a separate cyberattack targeting the FBI.
Clayton told the ABC News host that disruptions affecting Microsoft and other major institutions arose following necessary system upgrades rather than coordinated cyberattacks, while refusing to disclose specifics about the breach of an FBI crime database reported Saturday. The intelligence chief warned that Americans should expect additional outages as companies and government agencies modernize outdated systems amid an increase in cyberattacks.
“Let me tell you what we know and be very clear with the American people,” Clayton said. “The incidents that we saw during the course of this week, we know that they were not coordinated and that they were not state-sponsored. These were what I would say is delays, outages, and the like resulting from upgrades to systems which are absolutely necessary. Going forward, we are going to see a lot more of that from companies and the government.”
WATCH:
This comes after a multitude of organizations and institutions from JP Morgan Chase to the National Security Agency (NSA) suffered from outages.
“We should all be transparent with the American people that we have dated systems in a highly evolving environment where they need to be upgraded in order to have cyber security,” he continued. “Now to your point on cyberattacks there, there is an increase, as I mentioned, in cyberattacks, but this is something that we have had for a long time.”

US tech outages: Intelligence chief Jay Clayton warns more issues likely as ageing systems are upgraded
US intelligence chief Jay Clayton warned that more tech outages may occur as systems undergo upgrades, amid recent disruptions and an FBI database hack probe.
The United States has experienced tech outages over the last week that affected several critical services. But last week might not be the end of outages, and more could take place in the coming days, US intelligence chief Jay Clayton warned.
Clayton, who has been serving as the Director of National Intelligence in the Trump administration since August 2026, spoke about the outages at CNN's State of the Union program. He said that they were caused by system upgrades and may happen again as agencies replace old systems.
“The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road,” he said.
Also read: AI data centres drive US construction jobs as skilled trades offer new career paths beyond college
“You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot. And as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service. That is going to happen."
Multiple government and corporate services experienced outage in the US in the last week. It includes an outage at the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) that brought flights across the US to a halt. A Microsoft outage followed, lasting several hours. Next, several US banks experienced service outages, followed by a brief disruption to the National Security Agency's network.
Also read: Bessent says Nvidia yet to answer US probe into alleged restricted AI chip sales to China
Clayton had addressed the issue earlier. On November 18, he said that tech outages are not connected to or part of a state-sponsored attack.
Earlier, Donald Trump had also attributed the tech failures to system upgrades. “We have thousands of companies that are upgrading right now, and when they upgrade, bad things happen,” he had said, emphasising at a White House presser on Friday that they were "separate."
FBI database breach
To add to the slew of recent tech outages, it was reported by CNN on Saturday that the FBI is investigating an apparent hack in the National Crime Information Centre (NCIC), its database that stores criminal records at the state and federal levels. The FBI has not confirmed the hack publicly.

sources.news_title: Top US Intel Official Says Americans Should Prepare for System Upgrades, Warns of ‘Bumps in the Road’
sources.text:
The United States’ top intelligence official on Sunday said that Americans should be prepared for system upgrades at companies and within government services, warning of possible “bumps in the road” following multiple nationwide outages this month.
In recent days, multiple companies and government agencies reported outages of services and communications networks. Microsoft, Apple, several major banks, and United Airlines reported outages over the past week or so, while the Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency have reported incidents.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday that Americans “should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems,” adding they “should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity.”
“And they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road. Any time you refurbish your house, upgrade any of your systems, there are going to be things that you do not expect,” he said, adding that companies and U.S. government agencies “are taking more systems down and putting them back up than ever before.”
In a separate interview with ABC News on Sunday, Clayton stressed that recent outages were not “coordinated” or “state-sponsored” cyberattacks on infrastructure and services.
“These were what I would say is delays, outages and the like resulting from upgrades to systems which are absolutely necessary going forward,” he remarked.
“And we’re going to see more of that. And companies and the government, we should all be transparent with the American people that we have dated systems in a highly evolving environment where they need to be upgraded in order to have cybersecurity.”
Microsoft cited, in part, a failure during a recent upgrade to its servers, spanning from what the company later determined was a “latent defect” in a network fix it had begun deploying over the summer.
Online banking troubles also piled up last week. JPMorgan Chase said that a software bug affected its internal hardware systems, which caused transactional delays for its customers and others sending money to related accounts, sending jitters throughout the financial system before the problem was resolved.
Meanwhile, the National Security Agency said an internal network it uses to communicate classified information experienced temporary degradation “during scheduled routine maintenance.”
The era of artificial intelligence, or AI, has also raised the stakes for internet security overall. As AI tools uncover new vulnerabilities, many other companies and institutions are racing to patch them before they can be targeted by hackers, a cat-and-mouse game that can lead to a different set of glitches.

US intelligence chief warns of more tech glitches amid system upgrades
US intelligence chief Jay Clayton warned Americans to expect further technology outages during system upgrades. He said the disruptions were inevitable as ageing infrastructure is modernised and cybersecurity strengthened.
Americans should expect more technology outages and service disruptions as companies and government agencies upgrade ageing systems, US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Sunday, warning that glitches are inevitable during the transition.
"During that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service. That is going to happen," Clayton told CNN's *State of the Union* programme.
Clayton's remarks came days after US President Donald Trump attributed a recent series of technology failures to companies upgrading their systems. The intelligence chief said the upgrades were necessary to improve system performance and strengthen cybersecurity as rapid technological advances put increasing pressure on older infrastructure.
A series of technology failures this month disrupted several critical US systems. These included a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage affecting email services, a technical glitch impacting several major banks and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network.
Speaking on ABC's *This Week*, Clayton reiterated that the outages were not caused by coordinated or state-sponsored attacks, maintaining that they were linked to technical upgrades.
However, he declined to comment on separate reports of cyberattacks targeting the FBI and the Department of Agriculture. He said he expected investigators to provide answers "in due course".

sources.news_title: Should you stock up to prepare for outages? The U.S. intelligence chief points to COVID as proof 'America is the most amazing and resilient place'
sources.text:
The country is on edge about the recent string of network outages, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tried to offer some reassurance but drew on an unsettling example.
Worried about an imminent catastrophe, many Americans are panic buying supplies at Costco and Walmart. In an interview on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday, Clayton was asked if it’s time to stock up to prepare for new, possibly extended, outages.
“America is the most amazing and resilient place, and we have been living with interruptions,” he replied. “Let’s give ourselves some credit. Let’s go back to COVID, other things. Americans fought their way through these terrible things in an incredible, resilient way.”
Wait, what?
During pandemic-era lockdowns, Americans frantically hoarded so many supplies that grocery stores had to ration necessities like toilet paper.
CNN’s Dana Bash immediately stopped him right there and asked if we could be in another COVID-like situation.
“Not at all, let me be clear. But what I’m saying is the American people are resilient,” Clayton reiterated, pointing out that officials and companies are being straightforward with what’s happening.
“I have such incredible faith in the American people. As we have this technological step change, we will handle it as a country,” he added.
But when pressed on what Americans should actually do to ensure their resilience, Clayton suggested that it’s enough to just be aware.
“How do you prepare? By knowing that systems are going to be upgraded,” he said. “They may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and the government are dealing with this on the front foot.”
The U.S. intelligence chief may not soothe many nerves by reminding people about COVID, as the number of outages at a wide range of places has stunned the country.
Last Thursday, Microsoft’s email and other office tools went down. Last Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all planes for more than four hours. It later blamed a copper wire that was being upgraded to a fiber-optic cable.
Day later, companies like Chase, Wells Fargo, United Airlines, and Apple saw temporary service disruptions. The National Security Agency’s internal classified communications network also suffered an outage, further fraying nerves.
U.S. officials, including Clayton, have said there’s no evidence of coordinated, state-sponsored attacks, suggesting network upgrades meant to patch vulnerabilities recently uncovered by AI were deployed hastily before all the bugs were worked out.
But reports also revealed that there have been cyberattacks elsewhere in recent days, including at the FBI and Agriculture Department. And last month saw so many cyberattacks that it was dubbed “Black October.”
Meanwhile, two officials at the Federal Emergency Management Agency told the Washington Post they were concerned about the outages and were having trouble believing they were a coincidence.
One official took out extra cash, and the other reported being bombarded with questions from former classmates asking whether they should prepare for an emergency.
“There is nothing on this scale that has happened before in this many sectors this close together,” one of the officials told the Post. “This is scary, and there is no leadership.”
Even before everything appeared to break down, Americans were already nervous after the Pentagon launched an initiative called FORTRESS, which seeks to ensure that every major U.S. military base can run for 90 days without outside help if a war cuts off power and supply chains.
Adding to the unease was the U.K. government’s campaign urging Britons to keep canned food, bottled water, and cash on hand to get through three days of disruption.
But in an interview with Fortune’s Catherina Gioino, Mark Giles, director of Downdetector parent company Ookla Research, said there’s nothing linking the outages.
“This is a big blip, but it’s kind of on par for the course for what we’re seeing in terms of those longer-term trends,” he explained. “Most of the time they’re fairly self-contained and remedied quite quickly. It’s the ones where you can’t withdraw money or you can’t access your emails that really get the headlines.”

"You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot," he said.
Clayton's warning came as the U.S. prepares to celebrate Thanksgiving on Thursday, one of the busiest travel weeks of the year. A technology outage prompted a nationwide ground stop just over a week ago, which lasted for hours.
The Federal Aviation Administration said router upgrades caused a flood of data that led to the ground stop, and that there is no indication of a cyberattack.
Separately, Microsoft said the Outlook outage was caused by "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade."
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent delivered a similar message on CBS' "Face the Nation."
Asked if Americans should be concerned about the security of their financial institutions, Bessent said: "No, they shouldn't."
"The patches may cause a glitch," he said, referring to measures banks are taking to safeguard from AI. "I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine; your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency."

“They have an incident. They’re dealing with it in the ordinary course,” Clayton said on ABC. “I’m sure we’ll get the answers in due course.” He said cyber incidents reported to the FBI have grown from roughly 750,000 in 2020 to more than a million.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was asked on CBS’ “Face the Nation” whether Americans should worry about their banks after last week’s glitches. “No, they shouldn’t,” he said, adding that security patches “may cause a glitch, which is what happened last week.”
“I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine,” Bessent said. “Your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency.”

sources.news_title: My washer and dryer outage
sources.text:
Everybody's talking about the recent outages and shutdowns. Our flights were canceled, our e-mail messages disappeared, and our national security was compromised.
So as a columnist who is laser-focused on stories that affect your life, I'm writing about the fact that my washer and dryer both met their maker (Whirlpool) during all this commotion.
The washer's agitator, a solid performer since 2004, was no longer its vibrant self. It was moving slowly, making a whining, grinding sound. In fairness, my wife helpfully commented that I too, often exhibit those same traits.
I did some research, and learned two things. First, it was the dogs' fault. It turns out that the agitators have small plastic pieces, referred to as “dogs,” that let the agitator grip in one direction, and spin freely in the other direction. The dogs are relatively inexpensive, but the directions to replace them are complicated, for me anyway. The work involves lots of parts removal and reassembly, and even a 7/16 inch socket wrench. In my house, if a repair job involves any tool other than a hammer or a screwdriver, I surrender. That's when the rule, “It'll probably cost less to buy a new one, than to get this ancient unit repaired,” goes into effect.
As I prepared to load the final wet load of wash into the dryer, whose service dates back to 2006, it too, began to cough and sputter. Now, I became agitated. Are you trying to tell me that, amid this current wave of national chaos, it is a coincidence that both of these fine appliances just stopped working at the same time? Could this be collusion? After all, they had been working side by side for decades. Legally, the dryer was now old enough to vote, and the washer could buy alcohol.
I asked Alexa, my in-house expert, “Why would a washer and dryer, consistently reliable for more than 20 years, begin to malfunction simultaneously?” She blamed the Biden administration.
With that mystery solved, my wife and I planned a trip to the big-box appliance store. First, we did our homework. It seems like these stores are ALWAYS having a sale. Lucky for us, our washer-dryer outage occurred just in time for their Fall Post-Halloween, Mid-November, Pre-Thanksgiving, Early Black Friday, Holiday Harvest, Pre-Christmas Blowout Extravaganza!
On the store's website, we found a washer and dryer with “sale” prices that snugly fit our budget. No bells, no whistles, and no digital controls designed to be understood only by MIT professors. No sir, these had old-timey knobs, as God intended. The plan was to go to the store, track down the appliance guru, and make the purchase. I had a couple of other items on my list, so my wife hit the appliance aisle first.
By the time I joined her, she had made a discovery. Those sale items were “okay,” but the smooth-talking sales rep had introduced her to a more expensive washer (also on sale!) with more capacity, an improved agitator, and noise reduction. You've heard the pitch before. “Sure, that other washer is fine. But for just a few hundred dollars more, you could have this one!”
I was torn. It was definitely a budget-buster, but I hadn't seen my wife's eyes that big since the time we went to a Braves-Yankees game, and she grabbed the binoculars when Derek Jeter stepped up to bat. We were behind home plate, in the front row.
I noticed the fancy washer had a 10-year parts warranty, which sounded impressive. When I asked the sales guy about it, he said, “Can I be honest?” Well, sure. Does that mean he had not been honest, up until now? Anyway, he said, “The parts that are covered under that warranty will last forever. It's the other parts that will break down first.” Now that's agitating. Is this progress?
It reminded me of when we bought a refrigerator last year. As we boasted to the installer that our previous fridge lasted 20-plus years, he laughed. “Well, I can guarantee you that won't happen again.”
So as America prepares to send a manned mission to Mars in 2032, I have a message for the astronauts. Ask about the warranty.
David Carroll is a Chattanooga journalist, and his latest book is "I Won't Be Your Escape Goat," available from his website, ChattanoogaRadioTV.com. You may contact him at RadioTV2020@yahoo.com.

sources.news_title: Americans Should Prepare For More Technological 'Bumps In The Road', National Intelligence Director Clayton Warns
sources.text:
Americans Should Prepare For More Technological ‘Bumps In The Road’, National Intelligence Director Clayton Warns
National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton warned that further technology outages may occur as aging systems are upgraded, while experts are urging businesses to strengthen disaster recovery and cybersecurity plans.
National Intelligence Director and White House AI Czar Jay Clayton suggested that there is a chance the country will witness more technological outages after a series of tech-related issues caused disruption to U.S. aviation, banking, national security communications and major online services.
"The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road," Clayton told CNBC on Sunday.
Analog-to-digital upgrades to an aging telecommunications network caused the Federal Aviation Administration to issue a nationwide ground stop order halting all departing flights for four hours on November 13.
Microsoft's servers became overloaded and shut down on November 12 after a system's update. Problems occurring during updates were also reportedly to blame for recent disruptions to the communications system used by the National Security Agency (NSA) and Apple services like iCloud and Apple Pay.
"You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot," Clayton clarified.
Cyber experts have also been telling people to prepare.
Associate Dean of Education for Computer Information Systems at California Institute of Applied Technology Dr. Adam J. Stark spoke to International Business Times about steps businesses should take to protect themselves against future disruptions.
"The initial step is to recognize how much of your business runs on a hosted platform. In particular, small businesses rely on outside providers for payments, scheduling, email and data storage ... The next step is to have a Disaster Recovery Plan in place. The plan should be communicated to everyone in the organization and tested on a regular basis," the expert said.
"Next, find your single points of failure and work to eliminate them. That includes technology, like relying on one internet connection or one payment processor. It also includes people. If only one employee knows how to restore your systems or get into a key account, that person is a single point of failure too," Stark added.
The growing risk of cyber attacks
Tech-focused outlets such as The Tech Buzz have pointed out that it is uncommon for the "nation's top intelligence official ... [to] weigh in on tech outages," but the recent high-profile interruptions are themselves unprecedented in their scale, frequency and importance.
Cyber attacks have also been on the rise. Although the majority of the most significant disruptions have not thus far been blamed on malicious cyber actors, major institutions and organizations including the FBI, the Department of Agriculture and JPMorgan Chase have been the subject of recent cyber attacks.
Clayton had previously told lawmakers that, while there was no evidence that the U.S. is on the receiving end of "a coordinated cyberattack or state-sponsored activity," the quickening pace of technological advancement outside the U.S.'s borders behooves Washington to prepare for the possibility of targeted cyber attacks.
Furthermore, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin warned Congress that both Iranian and North Korean cyber actors pose a threat to critical U.S. cyber infrastructure, a warning which is echoed by experts.
"It is well within Iran's cyber competencies to wage digital warfare at scale, using asymmetric, relatively low-sophistication tactics such as distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks, ransomware attacks, targeted attempts to disrupt critical infrastructure like electrical grids, water systems, energy systems, and transportation networks," Canada-based tech journalist and expert Carmi Levy told International Business Times.

sources.news_title: US Intelligence Chief Says Expect More Outages as Systems Are Rebuilt
sources.text:
US Intelligence Chief Says Expect More Outages as Systems Are Rebuilt
Americans should expect more technology outages and service disruptions as companies and government agencies replace ageing systems, the top US intelligence official said. Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence, told CNN that as part of that ongoing upgrade there would be glitches, gaps and interruptions in service, and that it was going to happen.
The remark is a forecast rather than an apology. Clayton said the upgrades were necessary to improve performance and cybersecurity, because technological advances are straining systems built for an earlier era, which puts a public warning where an assurance would normally sit.
And the month gives him his evidence. A string of failures has disrupted critical American systems, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that took out email services, a technical glitch that affected several major banks, and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network.
Clayton was interviewed on the weekend news programmes days after President Donald Trump attributed the same run of failures to upgrades of companies' technology systems, which is why the tone from both has been continuity rather than recovery.
On cause, he has been consistent. Speaking separately on ABC, Clayton reiterated his earlier statements that the outages were not the result of coordinated or state sponsored action, a conclusion he first set out in public days before the latest round of interviews.
And the two kinds of failure stayed separate in his answers. Asked about reports of cyberattacks on the FBI and the Department of Agriculture, Clayton declined to discuss the specifics and said he expected investigators to provide answers "in due course."
The reports he set aside are specific ones. CNN reported that the FBI's criminal information database had been hacked, and NBC News reported that the Department of Agriculture had been breached during the week, both stories carried by Reuters alongside his remarks.
That leaves two answers from the same round of interviews. The outages were not coordinated or state sponsored, a conclusion he has now given twice, and the breaches are for investigators, who he said would provide answers in due course.
- The US Director of National Intelligence expects more outages during upgrades
- Clayton said upgrades are needed for performance and cybersecurity
- Recent failures hit air travel, Microsoft email, major banks and the NSA network
- He said the outages were not coordinated or state sponsored
- He declined to discuss reported cyberattacks on the FBI and the Department of Agriculture
Source: Reuters

sources.news_title: Recent Major IT Security Breaches
sources.text:
Recent Major IT Security Breaches
By Jerry Lawson
It’s too early to determine the causes of the recent IT failures at the FAA, Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, the NSA, Apple, and other organizations. The Wall Street Journal, NBC News, and others have offered theories. Preliminary explanations exist, but they conflict, and the full root-cause analyses aren’t in.
Consider a few unconvincing explanations so far: FAA officials claimed a single bad router in Arkansas caused the national calamity. Microsoft blamed a latent software bug that surfaced under heavy traffic. The NSA said its network went down during scheduled maintenance. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton instead pointed to patches for software flaws that AI helped discover, yet the FAA administrator says there is “zero evidence of anything AI-related.”
I don’t claim to know what is going on, but there is one obvious candidate cause for the failures: 
Misplaced federal government priorities. Since early 2025, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has lost a third of its workforce through layoffs, buyouts, and early retirements. 
Is there a causal relationship? I don’t know. But it’s completely reasonable to suspect that losing so much experienced technical talent increased the risk.
What should the rest of us do in the meantime? Assume it will happen again. Have a backup way to reach clients and colleagues if email goes dark. Keep critical documents where you can get to them offline. Have a Plan B before your next flight. And urge your representatives in Congress to insist on real oversight of how these agencies are staffed and run.
For the sake of the national economy—and our personal wallets—we as a nation should insist that the people hired to rebuild these agencies are chosen for proven competence, not politics.

sources.text:

The country is on edge about the recent string of network outages, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tried to offer some reassurance but drew on an unsettling example.
Worried about an imminent catastrophe, many Americans are panic buying supplies at Costco and Walmart. In an interview on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday, Clayton was asked if it’s time to stock up to prepare for new, possibly extended, outages.
“America is the most amazing and resilient place, and we have been living with interruptions,” he replied. “Let’s give ourselves some credit. Let’s go back to COVID, other things. Americans fought their way through these terrible things in an incredible, resilient way.”
Wait, what?
During pandemic-era lockdowns, Americans frantically hoarded so many supplies that grocery stores had to ration necessities like toilet paper.
CNN’s Dana Bash immediately stopped him right there and asked if we could be in another COVID-like situation.
“Not at all, let me be clear. But what I’m saying is the American people are resilient,” Clayton reiterated, pointing out that officials and companies are being straightforward with what’s happening.
“I have such incredible faith in the American people. As we have this technological step change, we will handle it as a country,” he added.
But when pressed on what Americans should actually do to ensure their resilience, Clayton suggested that it’s enough to just be aware.
“How do you prepare? By knowing that systems are going to be upgraded,” he said. “They may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and the government are dealing with this on the front foot.”
The U.S. intelligence chief may not soothe many nerves by reminding people about COVID, as the number of outages at a wide range of places has stunned the country.
Last Thursday, Microsoft’s email and other office tools went down. Last Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all planes for more than four hours. It later blamed a copper wire that was being upgraded to a fiber-optic cable.
Day later, companies like Chase, Wells Fargo, United Airlines, and Apple saw temporary service disruptions. The National Security Agency’s internal classified communications network also suffered an outage, further fraying nerves.
U.S. officials, including Clayton, have said there’s no evidence of coordinated, state-sponsored attacks, suggesting network upgrades meant to patch vulnerabilities recently uncovered by AI were deployed hastily before all the bugs were worked out.
But reports also revealed that there have been cyberattacks elsewhere in recent days, including at the FBI and Agriculture Department. And last month saw so many cyberattacks that it was dubbed “Black October.”
Meanwhile, two officials at the Federal Emergency Management Agency told the Washington Post they were concerned about the outages and were having trouble believing they were a coincidence.
One official took out extra cash, and the other reported being bombarded with questions from former classmates asking whether they should prepare for an emergency.
“There is nothing on this scale that has happened before in this many sectors this close together,” one of the officials told the Post. “This is scary, and there is no leadership.”
Even before everything appeared to break down, Americans were already nervous after the Pentagon launched an initiative called FORTRESS, which seeks to ensure that every major U.S. military base can run for 90 days without outside help if a war cuts off power and supply chains.
Adding to the unease was the U.K. government’s campaign urging Britons to keep canned food, bottled water, and cash on hand to get through three days of disruption.
But in an interview with Fortune’s Catherina Gioino, Mark Giles, director of Downdetector parent company Ookla Research, said there’s nothing linking the outages.
“This is a big blip, but it’s kind of on par for the course for what we’re seeing in terms of those longer-term trends,” he explained. “Most of the time they’re fairly self-contained and remedied quite quickly. It’s the ones where you can’t withdraw money or you can’t access your emails that really get the headlines.”

sources.news_title: Doomsday Economy: Americans Turn to Survival Supplies Amid Growing Fears of Tech Outages
sources.text:
A growing number of Americans are spending more on emergency preparedness products as recent technological disruptions fuel concerns about the vulnerability of essential services and the possibility of widespread infrastructure failures.
From non-perishable food and bottled water to emergency power alternatives and survival kits, consumers are increasingly preparing for scenarios in which electricity, banking systems and digital communications could become unavailable for extended periods.
The trend, increasingly described as the "Emergency Economy" or "Doomsday Economy," reflects a shift in consumer behavior driven by concerns over AI-powered cyber threats, potential disruptions to the US electricity grid and growing uncertainty surrounding critical infrastructure.
Technical Disruptions Fuel Fears of Widespread Outages
A series of high-profile technical failures in recent weeks has heightened public anxiety across the United States, disrupting airline operations, interrupting email services and delaying banking transactions.
Although US authorities have dismissed rumors suggesting that a malicious actor was responsible for the incidents, concerns about the possibility of broader technological disruptions have continued to influence consumer decisions.
In Houston, some residents has begun preparing her household for potential emergencies by purchasing liquefied petroleum gas and fire-starting supplies to ensure her family can cook and stay warm without electricity.
They have also replenished stocks of non-perishable food, hygiene products and allergy medication, preparing for the possibility that her family could remain at home for several days.
Their prioritycis ensuring her family has access to food, water and basic security during a prolonged disruption, according to CNBC.
Emergency Preparedness Spending Surges Nearly 400%
The growing appetite for emergency supplies is translating into a significant commercial opportunity.
Consumer spending at brands specializing in emergency preparedness products increased approximately 400% between November 12 and 17 compared with the same period last year, according to data from Consumer Edge.
Ready America, a company specializing in survival kits, emergency water supplies and high-calorie food products, recorded an almost fivefold increase in online sales in recent days.
Demand has also expanded beyond individual households, with businesses and institutions increasing orders for backup supplies intended for office environments.
Ready America CEO Trevin Rees said the company had not experienced comparable demand since the COVID-19 lockdown period more than six years ago.
The surge has forced the company to ask suppliers to increase production to keep pace with orders.
However, the rapid increase in demand has already created shortages of certain products, including water purification tablets, prompting the company to direct customers toward alternatives such as pre-packaged emergency water pouches.
Geopolitical Tensions Add to the Preparedness Boom
The increase in emergency spending did not begin with the latest wave of technical disruptions.
Consumer Edge data indicate that demand for preparedness products had already started rising weeks earlier.
Interest accelerated toward the end of last month following reports that the US Department of Defense was preparing to operate military bases for up to 90 days without external support.
The war involving Iran has also contributed to concerns among some consumers, reinforcing interest in household security and emergency planning.
Firearms sales in October increased approximately 8% compared with the same month last year, according to the National Shooting Sports Foundation (NSSF).
Retailers and manufacturers have also reported continued strong demand throughout November.
Mark Oliva, the NSSF's managing director of public affairs said consumers were expressing their priorities through spending on products they believe could help protect themselves and their families.
Wall Street Tracks the Rise of the Doomsday Economy
The growing preparedness trend has attracted attention from financial institutions seeking to understand how consumer anxiety is influencing spending patterns.
Mizuho Financial Group identified concerns surrounding technological disruptions and what it described as social media-driven "end-of-the-world" fears as factors contributing to increased shopping activity at Costco.
The financial group projected that Costco's comparable sales growth, excluding fuel, could exceed 10% in November for the first time since 2022.
RBC also noted that disaster preparedness had begun influencing purchasing behavior across global markets in recent weeks.
However, the increase has been concentrated primarily in specific categories, including long-life food products, water purification supplies and dry food staples.
The findings suggest that emergency preparedness is becoming more than a niche consumer activity, with its effects increasingly visible in retail performance and broader market analysis.
Gold and Cybersecurity Emerge as Potential Beneficiaries
The trend is also extending into financial assets and digital security.
American Hartford Gold reported an increase in customer inquiries during the week, as some consumers showed greater interest in gold as a safe-haven asset.
Company President Max Baecker said some customers had become more interested in precious metals following a technical disruption affecting JPMorgan Chase services that interrupted customer transactions for several hours.
Meanwhile, concerns about cyber vulnerabilities have moved higher on the US political and security agenda.
Vice President JD Vance cancelled his participation in a New York Times event to attend meetings related to the technical disruptions.
National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton, however, said the recent incidents were not the result of a cyberattack or a coordinated operation by a foreign government.
Senator Mark Warner, vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, warned that Americans were becoming increasingly concerned about the country's cyber vulnerabilities.
He added that the United States had so far been fortunate not to experience a major AI-powered cyberattack.
Cybersecurity Companies Could Benefit from Rising Corporate Investment
Growing concerns about artificial intelligence and the potential misuse of advanced technologies could create additional opportunities for cybersecurity companies.
Bilal Hafiz, CEO of Macro Hive expects concerns about AI systems potentially operating beyond human control to encourage businesses to accelerate investment in digital security.
Market performance has already provided some indication of investor interest.
The Global X Cybersecurity ETF gained approximately 3% over the previous two weeks, moving against the broader decline affecting AI stocks and the technology sector.
The divergence highlights how growing concerns over digital vulnerabilities could redirect investment toward companies developing tools to protect networks, systems and critical infrastructure.
A Return to Traditional Survival Methods
The preparedness boom is also visible in online search activity.
Google searches for emergency preparedness-related terms have doubled compared with the same period last year, while YouTube searches for survival-related content have surged by more than 5,000%.
For some households, the trend represents a return to basic methods of managing daily life without relying entirely on digital infrastructure.
The Doomsday Economy: A New Consumer Spending Trend?
The growing demand for emergency supplies highlights how technological dependence, geopolitical uncertainty and fears of cyber threats can reshape consumer behavior.
While recent disruptions have not been established as evidence of a coordinated attack, their impact on public confidence is becoming increasingly visible in purchasing patterns.
From emergency food and water to gold investments and cybersecurity services, businesses across several industries are positioning themselves to benefit from a market increasingly shaped by preparedness.
